turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does a firefly make its own light—not just reflect light from somewhere else? Our three fictional specialists are Mira Venn, an enzyme biochemist; Tomas Rell, who studies insect cells; and Leena Sorel, whose field is molecular light emission. Tomas, let’s begin inside the insect: what are the light-producing cells, and how do they give us a starting point?

turns.speaker: expert2
turns.text:
The light-producing cells are called photocytes, and they form part of a specialised tissue—the light organ. In the adult firefly Aquatica leii, for example, the organ has a distinct light-producing layer containing these cells.

There’s also a useful link to the chemistry. A separate microscopy study used antibody-based labels to locate luciferase—the enzyme involved in light production—in tiny granules within photocytes. So we’re not just looking at tissue that happens to glow; we can locate some of its molecular machinery.

That tells us where the enzyme is found. It doesn’t yet explain how a chemical reaction produces light.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Mira, we’ve located the enzyme in those cells. What does it help happen? Walk us from the reacting molecule to light, keeping the jobs of luciferin, luciferase, ATP and oxygen distinct.
